concept.name: Iron condor
concept.definition: An iron condor is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining an out-of-the-money bull put spread (long lower put, short higher put) and an out-of-the-money bear call spread (short lower call, long higher call), all at four different strikes. The standard ('short') iron condor is entered for a net credit and profits maximally when the underlying finishes between the two short strikes.
concept.intuition: It is a short strangle with the tails cut off: you sell options on both sides of the market but buy further-out options as wings, so your worst case is fixed.
concept.mechanics: Net credit = total premium sold minus premium bought; maximum gain is the credit between the short strikes; maximum loss is the wider wing width minus the credit, realized beyond either long strike. 'Iron' indicates the structure mixes calls and puts, unlike an all-call or all-put condor.
concept.formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = wing width - net credit; breakevens = short put strike - credit and short call strike + credit.
concept.failure_modes: Losses are a multiple of the credit, so a few full-wing losses erase many wins; with four legs, bid-ask slippage and commissions are material, and expiration pin risk on a short strike can leave an unwanted stock position over the weekend.
concept.misconceptions: Defined risk does not mean low risk of ruin: selling far-OTM wings for a 'high probability' condor still concentrates tail exposure. The credit is not income; it is the price of bearing the bounded loss.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100: buy $90 put, sell $95 put, sell $105 call, buy $110 call for a $1.80 net credit. Max gain $180 if XYZ finishes between $95 and $105; max loss $320 beyond either wing.
